content: Preterm birth is a significant contributor to perinatal mortality and morbidity. Cyclo-oxygenase (COX) inhibitors are medications that suppress uterine contractions, are relatively easy to administer, and are associated with minimal maternal side effects. However, there have been reports of adverse effects on the fetus and newborn following exposure to these drugs. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of COX inhibitors, used as tocolytic agents, on maternal and neonatal outcomes. The comparison was made against placebo, no intervention, or other tocolytic agents. Additionally, the review aimed to compare the effects of non-selective COX inhibitors with COX-2 selective inhibitors. The search for relevant studies included the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register (as of August 24, 2014), consultation with experts, and examination of reference lists from retrieved studies. The inclusion criteria were randomized trials, both published and unpublished, that investigated the use of COX inhibitors for tocolysis in women between 20 and 36 weeks of gestation. Two independent reviewers assessed the methodological quality of the studies and extracted data. Additional information was sought from study authors when necessary. Results were presented using risk ratios (RR) for dichotomous data and mean differences (MD) for continuous data, both with 95% confidence intervals (CI). The number needed to treat for benefit (NNTB) and the number needed to treat for harm (NNTH) were calculated for statistically significant categorical outcomes. The review included 20 studies involving 1,509 women, with seven new studies (684 women) added since the previous review. The non-selective COX inhibitor indomethacin was the most commonly studied drug, used in 15 of the included studies. The overall quality of the studies was rated as moderate to low. Three small studies (102 women), two of which were conducted in the 1980s, compared indomethacin with placebo. These studies showed no significant difference in the rate of birth within 48 hours of trial entry (average RR 0.20, 95% CI 0.03 to 1.28; two studies, 70 women). However, one small study (36 women) demonstrated that indomethacin reduced the risk of preterm birth before 37 weeks of gestation (RR 0.21, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.62; NNTB 2, 95% CI 2 to 4). Indomethacin was also associated with an increase in gestational age at birth (average MD 3.59 weeks, 95% CI 0.65 to 6.52; two studies, 66 women) and birthweight (MD 716.34 g, 95% CI 425.52 to 1007.16; two studies, 67 infants). No significant differences were observed in neonatal morbidity or mortality. When compared with betamimetics, COX inhibitors reduced the likelihood of birth within 48 hours of trial entry (RR 0.27, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.96; NNTB 7, 95% CI 6 to 120; two studies, 100 women) and preterm birth before 37 weeks of gestation (RR 0.53, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.99; NNTB 6, 95% CI 4 to 236; two studies, 80 women). However, no improvements were observed in neonatal morbidity or mortality. COX inhibitors were associated with fewer maternal adverse effects compared to betamimetics (RR 0.19, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.31; NNTB 3, 95% CI 2 to 3; five studies, 248 women) and fewer maternal adverse effects requiring treatment cessation (average RR 0.09, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.49; NNTB 5, 95% CI 5 to 9; three studies, 166 women). No significant differences were found when comparing COX inhibitors with magnesium sulfate (MgSO4) (seven studies, 792 women) or calcium channel blockers (CCBs) (two studies, 230 women) in terms of prolonging pregnancy or fetal/neonatal outcomes. There were also no differences in the rate of very preterm birth (before 34 weeks of gestation), and no maternal deaths were reported in the one study that assessed this outcome. However, COX inhibitors were associated with fewer maternal adverse effects compared to MgSO4 (RR 0.39, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.62; NNTB 11, 95% CI 9 to 17; five studies, 635 women). A comparison of non-selective COX inhibitors with COX-2 selective inhibitors (two studies, 54 women) did not reveal any differences in maternal, fetal, or neonatal outcomes. No data were available to compare COX inhibitors with oxytocin receptor antagonists (ORAs). Additionally, there were no data on extremely preterm birth (before 28 weeks of gestation), long-term infant outcomes, or cost-effectiveness. The authors concluded that there is no clear evidence to support the superiority of COX inhibitors over placebo or other tocolytic agents. While some benefits were observed, such as delaying birth and reducing maternal adverse effects compared to betamimetics and MgSO4, the evidence is limited by small sample sizes, minimal safety data, lack of long-term outcomes, and generally low study quality. Further well-designed studies are needed to evaluate the shortand long-term benefits of COX inhibitors compared to placebo and other tocolytics, particularly CCBs and ORAs. Future research should also focus on determining whether COX-2 selective inhibitors are superior to non-selective COX inhibitors. Additionally, studies should assess long-term outcomes into early childhood and consider cost-effectiveness.
